question.text: A non-conducting ring of radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>5</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> carries the total charge of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1.11</mn><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></msup><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math>, distributed non-uniformly on its circumference, producing an electric field everywhere in space. The value of the line integral <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><munderover><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>∞</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><mo>-</mo><mi>E</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> being centre of the ring) in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>volt</mi></math> is

solution.text:
By definition, ∫l=∞l=0-E→.dl→=V, the potential at the centre of the ring.

V=14πε0.QR=9×109×1.11×10-100.5=2 V

Hence, the value of the given line integral is 2 V
